3.0.0.en: Although Naomi found her sustenance from Ruth's labor in gathering ears every day, which sufficed her and was more than enough, yet in love she wanted stability and a better life for Ruth, and she told her so.

3.1.0.en: Winnoweth: the process of winnowing is the separation of the grains of barley from the straw.

3.1.1.en: Threshingfloor: a wide place where the processes of threshing and winnowing are carried out to separate the grain from the straw, and then the grain is gathered into the storehouse.

3.1.2.en: Naomi reminded Ruth that Boaz is a relative of hers through her husband, and consequently he could marry her and she would settle into a happy life. And the day is suitable for meeting him, because it is a day of joy with the winnowing and gathering of the barley crop on the threshingfloor. And the relative is the kinsman whom the Law calls to marry the wife of the deceased, and the firstborn son is reckoned to the deceased, and thereby he raises up offspring for him (Deut 25:5-10).

3.2.0.en: Naomi asked Ruth to take off the clothes of her widowhood and to prepare to be in the most beautiful appearance by washing and anointing herself with perfumes and putting on the best she had, then to go to the threshingfloor of Boaz but to hide herself so that no one would know of her presence, and to watch him from afar until he had finished eating and drinking, that is, had taken his supper, before he lay down.

3.2.1.en: And Ruth's preparation to be like a bride for Boaz signifies the preparation of the human soul that wants to enjoy Christ: it must wash, that is, receive the sacrament of Baptism, and then be anointed, that is, receive the sacrament of the Holy Myron with the holy oil. And after it receives the new nature and the Holy Spirit dwells in it, it puts on the garments of righteousness, that is, puts on Christ, and then it can be before Him on the threshingfloor, where the grain is separated from the straw, which signifies the Day of Judgment. But because the soul is prepared, it rejoices in this day when it meets its Bridegroom, who judges the world, and He takes it to be His bride. This Bridegroom is Christ, whom Boaz signifies.

3.3.0.en: She said to her, notice the place where he goes and sleeps, and after making sure that he is asleep, go and lie down at his feet. And this practice was well known, for slaves and maidservants used to sleep at the feet of their masters so as to serve them if they wished during the night. In addition, Ruth is a devout person and Boaz likewise a righteous man, and the purpose of Ruth's act was that Boaz might feel his responsibility and his duty as kinsman toward her so as to marry her, and not any lustful purpose, especially since the difference in age was great between the young woman Ruth and the older man Boaz.

3.4.0.en: Ruth's obedience to Naomi appears, although the words of the Jewish Law were new to her, but in confidence in her mother-in-law's love for her she obeyed, bearing any risks that might meet her or any bad treatment that she might face.

3.4.1.en: May you think of the comfort of those around you before your own comfort, and if you accustom yourself to this in your youth, you can keep the spirit of giving and sacrifice however old you grow and become needy and weak, and you will continue to think of what to give your strong children, and then you will experience the mercies of God and His countless gifts.

3.5.s.en: (2) Ruth lies down at Boaz's feet

3.5.0.en: The heap of corn: heaps of sheaves of barley stored at the edge of the threshingfloor.

3.5.1.en: Ruth obeyed all of Naomi's words and went to the threshingfloor of Boaz, and after he finished eating and drinking, and his heart was of course glad at the new harvest, he went to sleep in a tent or small hut that had been made for him beside the heaps of sheaves of barley at the side of the threshingfloor. And after he had fallen deeply asleep and the workers on the threshingfloor had also slept, Ruth slipped in quietly and uncovered his feet and lay down and covered herself with the edge of his covering, to declare to him that just as his feet were uncovered of the covering, so she too needs someone to cover her and marry her and carry out the commandment of the Jewish Law and raise up offspring for her dead husband.

3.6.0.en: Spread therefore thy skirt: cover me with the edge of your garment, that is, offer me your care and your protection and your covering by marrying me, so as to carry out the Law and raise up offspring for my dead husband.

3.6.1.en: In the middle of the night Boaz turned in his sleep and felt the presence of someone at his feet, so he was startled and asked, who is sleeping at my feet?.. So Ruth, who had been awake all night, hurried, and perhaps she had been praying during these hours that God would prosper her way and give her grace in the eyes of Boaz so that he would not rebuke her or reject her, and she answered him that she was Ruth his handmaid, and asked him to cover her as a kinsman and marry her and care for her in order to raise up offspring for her dead husband. And this action shows many virtues in Ruth, namely:

3.6.2.en: 1- Her obedience to her mother-in-law despite the difficulty of the responsibility.

3.6.3.en: 2- Her humility in saying that she was his handmaid.

3.6.4.en: 3- Her courage in facing this difficult situation

3.6.5.en: 4- Her love of God and obedience to His Law, so she set aside every earthly desire to marry a young man and asked for the carrying out of the word of God.

3.6.6.en: And Ruth signifies the soul that is alone with Christ in the night to pray and to contemplate His beauty and to ask for His care for it and its union with Him in love.

3.7.0.en: Boaz praised her for two things:

3.7.1.en: 1- Her first kindness, which was her leaving her family and her people and her gods to accompany her mother-in-law and embrace her religion and live among her people.

3.7.2.en: 2- Her second kindness, which is the greater, by which she wanted to raise up offspring for her dead husband by marrying an old man, Boaz, and she was not preoccupied with young men, poor or rich, to satisfy her human desires.

3.7.3.en: Be occupied with the love of God and His commandments, and you will enjoy fellowship with Him before you seek your material needs and your lawful desires, because the love of God satisfies the soul, and He then provides for all the needs of the body.

3.8.0.en: The gate of my people: that is, all the families living in houses that have doors, and it means all the people of the city.

3.8.1.en: Boaz then reassured Ruth that he had the right of kinsmanship and care for her, and praised her as a virtuous woman, and all the people of the city agree on this because of what she did for her mother-in-law.

3.9.0.en: Boaz informed Ruth that he is a kinsman and ready to perform the right of a kinsman, but there is a kinsman nearer than he. And this shows Boaz's carefulness in carrying out the Law of God, for he did not use his influence to achieve what he was convinced of, for he is also a devout man who knows how to carry out the Law.

3.10.0.en: Boaz permitted Ruth to stay the night on the threshingfloor until morning because she could not return to her house during the night, and in the morning Boaz would summon the nearer kinsman to do his duty and marry Ruth and redeem the field of Elimelech her father-in-law, which was mortgaged, which he had mortgaged because of his poverty before he emigrated to Moab (ch. 4:3, 4). And Boaz confirmed his words with an oath, which was well known at that time, namely "as the LORD liveth," that he would fulfill this matter and summon the nearer kinsman, and if he did not perform his duties, he himself would perform the right of a kinsman.

3.11.0.en: Ruth lay at the side of the threshingfloor until morning, and at the beginning of dawn, before anyone could distinguish from afar the features of any person, Boaz called her to return to her house, and out of respect for her standing he said to her, let no one know that you came to the threshingfloor, so that it might be clear that he is the one who performed the right of a kinsman of his own accord, although it would not have been wrong for her to demand her right, but he tried to give her a better standing, and on the other hand so that no one would think that there was some shameful act between a man and a woman, although the piety of Boaz and Ruth is evident, yet he is careful in everything. And his private servant may have awakened, and Boaz informed him not to tell anyone of the coming of a woman to the threshingfloor.

3.12.0.en: Before Ruth departed, Boaz wanted to honor her, so he asked her to bring her outer garment, which is like a cloak or a wrap that is wrapped over the clothes, and then he put in it six measures of barley. And what is meant by this measure is most likely the omer, which equals about 1.75 kg, that is, he gave her about 10.5 kg of grains of barley, and she tied it up in this garment, and then Boaz helped her tenderly and placed it on her shoulders for her to return with it to her mother-in-law. And Ruth departed, returning to Naomi, and then a little later Boaz also arose and entered the city to summon the kinsman and come to an understanding with him.

3.13.0.en: Ruth reached her mother-in-law's house at the beginning of dawn, and her mother-in-law was deeply asleep, so when she heard knocking on the door and the voice of a woman speaking to her, she asked her who she was, because she had not yet fully awakened from her sleep. So she told her that she was Ruth, and then she hurried to open to her, and Ruth entered and told her everything that had happened in detail.

3.14.0.en: Ruth also told her mother-in-law of the generosity of Boaz, who gave her a large quantity of barley.

3.15.0.en: Naomi was confident of the love of God and the nobility and piety of Boaz, so she reassured Ruth, saying to her, sit still and rest, for God will provide good, and the devout Boaz will not rest until he has completed your marriage.

3.15.1.en: In the most difficult situations be assured that God provides good for you however adverse matters may seem, for He turns them to your good and will not neglect you until you feel rest and peace in His hands.

4.0.s.en: (1) The dialogue of Boaz with the nearer kinsman

4.0.0.en: It appears that the gate of the city of Bethlehem was higher than the rest of the city, so Boaz went up to it. And at the gate there is a square where the leaders of the people sit to judge the affairs of the city, and there the men of the city pass by to go out to their work. So out of Boaz's concern to complete the matter for Ruth, he went there early.

4.1.0.en: The Law provides that every word shall be established at the mouth of two or three witnesses (Deut 17:6), but Boaz here called a larger number to confirm and establish what was done, and the number ten also indicates completeness. And he called them from among the elders whose opinion is respected in the matters concerning the city.

4.2.0.en: When a famine occurred in Bethlehem and Elimelech became poor, he mortgaged his land for a sum of money to provide for his material needs; then he traveled to Moab, and with his death and the death of his two sons his land became the property of his wife Naomi and the wife of his son, Ruth, because Orpah, the wife of the second son, remained in Moab and perhaps she had married one of the pagans of her people in her country. Therefore Ruth sells her land, meaning she needs someone to pay the mortgage and recover the land of her husband and her father-in-law.

4.2.1.en: And two things were required, the first the redeeming of the land and the second marriage to Ruth. And Boaz began by presenting the first matter to the kinsman before the elders, which was the redeeming of the land, and afterward he would present to him the second requirement.

4.3.0.en: Boaz and the kinsman and the ten elders sat in the square in front of the gate of the city, and others of the people came to this presentation of the case, and Boaz asked the kinsman nearer to Ruth to redeem her land, that is, to pay the price of the mortgage and restore the land, and if he could not, then Boaz is the second kinsman and he is ready to redeem the land. So the first kinsman answered, declaring his agreement to redeem the land, and his purpose in this was to enlarge his properties so as to use this land to increase his production and his wealth.

4.4.0.en: After the first kinsman agreed to redeem the land, Boaz asked of him the second requirement, which is linked to the first, namely marriage to Ruth so that he might raise up by her offspring ascribed to her husband and her father-in-law, and in this way the name and inheritance of Elimelech would not be cut off in Israel.

4.5.0.en: The first kinsman refused to redeem the land when he found himself obliged to marry Ruth, and he stated that the reason is that by redeeming the land he would mar his own inheritance. He means that he would buy a land, paying the price of its mortgage, and then it would become the property of Ruth's son, and his other sons would take nothing from it, because the man was married and had sons. So he would pay money and then the inheritance would pass to his son by Ruth who would be ascribed to Elimelech. In this he did not think of fulfilling the Law by raising up a son for his dead relative, but thought only of his possessions, and did not want to spend money or effort from which he would not reap an inheritance for his children, because his new son by Ruth would be ascribed to Elimelech. So it is clear that he loves money more than he loves fulfilling the Law and helping others. And in the end he said to Boaz, redeem for yourself the land of Elimelech and marry Ruth, for I will not marry her.

4.6.0.en: The Law provided in (Deut 25:7-10) that the kinsman who refuses to marry the wife of the dead man to raise up offspring for him is to take off his sandal and give it to the kinsman who follows him, as a declaration of his giving up his responsibility. And the taking off of the sandal signifies the inability of this kinsman, who takes off the sandal, to tread on the land of the deceased, which he refused to buy, leaving the next kinsman after him to redeem the land and tread on it. Therefore Moses took off his sandal before God in the bush, and the priests and deacons take off their sandals when they enter the sanctuary, to declare that they are not the true Bridegroom, but Christ is the Good Shepherd and they are His servants. For He is the true Kinsman of our souls, who bought us with His blood on the Cross, and it is He who brings us into our new land, that is, the Kingdom of Heaven, and He bought it and prepared it for us and entered it after He completed our redemption to declare that we have entry into it through our faith and our life with Him.

4.7.0.en: The first kinsman declared his refusal to redeem the land and marry Ruth, so he took off his sandal before the elders as the Law provides, and by this declaration it became Boaz's right to marry Ruth and redeem the land. And Boaz here signifies Christ, who marries His Church and raises up from her many children, and redeems, that is, pays all the debts of sin, for His bride.

4.7.1.en: Do not be occupied with the love of money, because it passes away, but use it to win the love of others and to show mercy to the needy, for this is what remains to you and with it you enter eternity.

4.8.s.en: (2) The marriage of Boaz to Ruth

4.8.0.en: Boaz affirmed before the elders and all who were gathered at the gate of the city that he now had the right of kinsmanship over Ruth, since the first kinsman had given it up, so he can now redeem the land.

4.9.0.en: The gate of his place: it means the gate of the city of Bethlehem, that is, the name of Elimelech will be remembered in Bethlehem because he has offspring.

4.9.1.en: Likewise it is Boaz's right to marry Ruth and raise up offspring by her, so that the memory of Elimelech may not be cut off in Israel.

4.9.2.en: So that no misunderstanding occurs between you and others, when you agree on something, may you confirm it in specific and clear words. That is, be exact in your speech and specific so as to keep your peace with others.

4.10.0.en: The elders and those present declared their agreement that Boaz should become the kinsman able to marry Ruth and redeem the land, and that they were witnesses to this agreement, and they even declared their wishes and good prayer for him that Ruth would be to Boaz like Leah and Rachel, by whom the people of the children of Israel were formed. That is, they wished for him good, blessed offspring from Ruth, and they also prayed for him to have strength in his spiritual and social life, which would appear in his city Ephratah, which is Bethlehem.

4.11.0.en: The elders also prayed for Boaz for strength and blessing like Pharez, who broke forth against Zarah his brother at their birth (Gen 38), and had strong offspring, and from him came Boaz. And this Pharez was the son of Judah by Tamar.

4.12.s.en: (3) David from the offspring of Ruth

4.12.0.en: After Boaz became the kinsman responsible for Ruth, he married her, and the blessing of God appeared for this person of foreign race whose heart was filled with love and faith in God and His Law, so He granted her to conceive and bear a son, and she called him Obed (v. 17). And here the emphasis is on Ruth, although Boaz too rejoiced in the grace of God in this newborn, because the son would be ascribed to Mahlon, the deceased husband of Ruth, and to his grandfather Elimelech.

4.12.1.en: The blessings of God are many for the weak who believe in Him and cry out to Him because they have no one but Him. So hold fast to God however difficult your circumstances, and trust that He will not leave you, but on the contrary He esteems all the works of your love and rewards you with blessings on earth and in heaven.

4.13.0.en: Not only did Ruth and Boaz rejoice in the newborn, but Naomi also rejoiced in him greatly, and the women of Bethlehem rejoiced with her, so they hurried to congratulate her on the newborn, whom they called "a kinsman," because through him the name of his father Mahlon and his grandfather Elimelech and also his grandmother Naomi would be remembered.

4.14.0.en: The women praised the newborn and told Naomi that through him her soul would be refreshed and rejoice, for through him she would have offspring and a name in Israel. And also when he grows up and Naomi becomes old, he will care for her and her need in her old age. And they praised Ruth, for they told Naomi that Ruth's love and care for her is better than having seven sons, who would not care for her as Ruth tends her and loves her, and consequently she should not grieve over the loss of her husband and her two sons, because Ruth has compensated her for them.

4.15.0.en: In the tenderness of motherhood, Naomi embraced the newborn and took care of his upbringing with his mother Ruth, and Naomi's neighbors shared her joy and chose a name for the newborn, "Obed," which means servant, that is, servant of God. Thus they wished that he would live in obedience to God as His servant and gladden the heart of his mother and father and grandmother. And the book mentions that Obed is the father of Jesse and the grandfather of David the prophet, from whom came Christ the Savior of the world.

4.15.1.en: And Obed signifies Christ, who humbled Himself by His Incarnation, taking the form of a servant to complete our redemption, and just as Ruth contained him in her womb, so Naomi took him in her arms. Thus everyone who receives Christ within him obtains salvation and joy, whether he is from the Jews or from the Gentiles, for He is the Savior of the whole world.

4.16.0.en: Pharez: he is the son of Judah the son of Jacob, whom he begot by Tamar (Gen 38). Hezron: a large clan came out of him (Gen 46:12; Num 26:6). Ram: he is Aram as mentioned in (Mt 1:3). Amminadab: he is the father of Elisheba the wife of Aaron (Ex 6:23). Nahshon: he is the brother of Elisheba the wife of Aaron and was the prince of the tribe of Judah in the days of Moses the prophet (Num 2:3, 10:14).

4.16.1.en: Salmon: one of the great men of Judah in the days of Joshua the son of Nun, and he married Rahab, who received the spies in Jericho.

4.16.2.en: And the rest of the names mentioned are well known and have been mentioned before, for these very names were mentioned in the genealogy of Christ in (Mt 1), and it may be that some names were omitted from this genealogy because of their little importance, or it may be that there are no omitted names.

4.16.3.en: And although the book began with a distress, which is the famine because of which Elimelech emigrated to Moab, it ends with happy news, which is the birth of Obed, from whose offspring came Christ, the Bread of Life and the Savior of the world. And this genealogy also shows the love of Christ and His humility, who came from the offspring of Ruth the Moabitess, and even from the offspring of Gentile women and even harlots like Rahab, for He honors women in general, since He mentioned in His genealogy all these, that is, Tamar and Ruth and Rahab, the Gentile women, in addition to Bathsheba, the Jewish wife of David, with whom he committed adultery. For Christ came to save the whole world, Jews and Gentiles, and to turn sinners into saints.
